q: Which of the following is TRUE about a futures contract?
o: Only the buyer pays initial margin
Only the seller pays initial margin
Both buyer and seller pay initial margin
No margin is required for futures
e: Both parties pay initial margin in a futures contract because both have an obligation to perform. The exchange enforces this; the clearing corporation guarantees settlement.

q: Basis is defined as:
o: Spot price plus Cost of carry
e: Basis = Spot − Futures. When futures > spot, basis is negative (a 'premium' or contango). At expiry, basis converges to zero because final settlement is at spot.

q: On expiry day, the basis of a futures contract is:
e: Basis converges to zero at expiry because the futures contract is finally settled at the closing spot price of the underlying.

q: Cost of carry for an equity futures contract is:
e: For equity, cost of carry = Interest paid to fund the position − Dividend received during the holding period. Storage cost applies to commodities, not financial assets.

q: Daily settlement price for a futures contract is calculated as the:
o: Last traded price of the futures contract
Volume-weighted average price of the last 30 minutes of futures trading
e: Daily settlement uses the volume-weighted average of the last 30 minutes of futures trading. If untraded in the last 30 min, a theoretical price F = S × e^(r × t) is used.

q: Final settlement price of a stock or index futures contract is:
o: Closing spot price of the underlying on expiry
Average futures price of the day before expiry
e: Final settlement is at the closing spot value of the underlying on expiry, which is why basis converges to zero at expiry.

q: After SEBI's revision effective November 20, 2024, the minimum value of a derivative contract at the time of introduction is:
e: SEBI raised the minimum derivative contract value to ₹15 lakh, with lot sizes set so the value at review stays in the ₹15-20 lakh band. The earlier band (set in 2015) was ₹5-10 lakh.

q: The number of futures contracts outstanding at a point in time is called:
e: Open interest is the cumulative number of unsettled contracts. Volume is the count of contracts traded in a window. OI changes only when a new position is created or an existing one is closed; transferring an existing position between two parties leaves OI unchanged.

q: If trader A had a short position and buys back to close, while trader E opens a new short of equal size, the open interest:
e: OI is unchanged: A's existing short position is transferred to E. The total outstanding contracts have not changed; only the identity of the short-side counterparty has.

q: If the spot price is ₹500, the risk-free rate is 6% p.a., and there are no dividends, the theoretical fair futures price for a 6-month contract (continuous compounding) is approximately:
The expiry day for monthly Nifty futures on NSE (per the May 2025 SEBI circular) is the:
o: Last working day of the month
First Friday of the next month
e: Per SEBI's May 2025 circular, each exchange must pick one expiry day. NSE selected last Tuesday for monthly Nifty (and weekly Nifty options). BSE chose last Thursday for monthly Sensex.

q: If the spot price of a stock is ₹200 and the cost of carry is ₹4 over a one-month period, the theoretical futures price is:
e: Theoretical futures price = Spot + Cost of carry = 200 + 4 = ₹204. Cost of carry already nets dividend out of interest cost.

q: Which margin is collected to cover the worst-case loss expected on a position over the next trading day?
e: Initial margin (computed using SPAN — Standard Portfolio Analysis of Risk) covers approximately 99% confidence loss over a one-day horizon. MTM settles realised daily P/L; exposure margin is an additional buffer above SPAN.

q: The MTM (mark-to-market) settlement for a futures contract happens:
o: Only on the day of trade
e: MTM happens daily — gains and losses are settled in cash on T+1 morning before market open, based on the day's settlement price.

q: A 'roll over' of a futures position involves:
o: Closing the near-month and simultaneously opening the next-month contract
Adding more contracts of the near month
Switching from a long to a short position
e: Roll over keeps the directional exposure beyond expiry. Long-side roll: sell the expiring contract and buy the next. Both legs simultaneously to manage basis risk.

q: Cash-and-carry arbitrage is profitable when:
o: Futures price is lower than fair value
Futures price is higher than fair value
e: When the futures price exceeds fair value (S × (1+r-d)^t), an arbitrageur can borrow, buy spot, sell the overpriced future, and lock in profit at expiry. The reverse (futures < fair value) requires shorting spot, which is constrained for stocks in India.

q: If you go long a Nifty futures contract at 24,000 (lot size 25) and pay 10% margin, your initial margin is approximately:
e: Contract value = 24,000 × 25 = ₹6,00,000. Initial margin at 10% = ₹60,000.

q: An 'open position' refers to:
o: Any executed trade in the day
An unsettled long or short position in a derivative contract
e: An open position is an outstanding (unsettled) buy or sell position in a contract — i.e. one that has not been closed by an offsetting trade or expiry settlement.

q: Tick size for Nifty futures is:
e: Nifty futures tick size is 5 paise — the minimum price increment allowed in quotations.

q: Which of these is NOT a feature standardised by the exchange in a futures contract?
e: Lot size, expiry, and tick size are all standardised. Price is determined by the buyer and seller through interaction in the order book — that's the only variable.

q: On the BSE, monthly Sensex futures expire on the:
o: Last Thursday of the contract month
Last Tuesday of the contract month
First Monday of the contract month
Last working day of the contract month
e: BSE chose the last Thursday as its uniform expiry day for monthly Sensex contracts and weekly Sensex options. NSE chose last Tuesday.

q: If the spot price of ABC Ltd is ₹100 and the one-year futures is trading at ₹108, while the fair value (with r=6%, d=2%) is ₹104, an arbitrageur should:
e: Futures (108) > fair (104), so cash-and-carry: borrow at 6%, buy spot at 100, sell futures at 108, deliver at expiry. Arbitrage profit = 108 - 104 = ₹4 per share, less transaction costs.

q: A 'price band' for a derivative contract refers to:
o: The range of prices at which the contract can be issued
The minimum and maximum prices the contract is allowed to trade at during the day
e: The price band is the daily trading range allowed, calculated relative to the previous day's close. Futures contracts use a ±10% operating range that triggers a price freeze (sent for confirmation), not auto-rejection.

q: Which of the following is TRUE about open interest and trading volume?
o: Open interest measures flow; volume measures snapshot
Open interest measures snapshot; volume measures flow
e: Open interest is the snapshot count of outstanding contracts at a point in time. Volume is the flow — number of contracts traded in a window. Identifying this distinction correctly is testable.
